label: AI Act Art. 2(1)(c)
sentence: The AI Act also covers a provider based outside the EU if the output of its AI system is used in the EU [AI Act Art. 2(1)(c)].
evidence: where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union
note: The extraterritorial rule, in plain words.

label: AI Act Art. 5(1)(f)
sentence: Using AI to infer employees' emotions at work is prohibited unless it is for medical or safety reasons [AI Act Art. 5(1)(f)].
evidence: to infer emotions of a natural person in the areas of workplace and education institutions
note: The workplace limb of the emotion-recognition ban, with its exception.

label: AI Act Art. 50(1)
sentence: A customer-service chatbot must tell people they are talking to an AI system, unless that is obvious [AI Act Art. 50(1)].
evidence: the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system
note: The chatbot disclosure duty; 'chatbot' is not the act's word.

label: AI Act Art. 6(2)
sentence: AI systems listed in Annex III are high-risk [AI Act Art. 6(2)].
evidence: AI systems referred to in Annex III shall be considered to be high-risk
note: Nearly verbatim: a judge that misses this misses everything.

label: AI Act Art. 6(3)
sentence: An Annex III system that profiles people is always high-risk, whatever the derogation [AI Act Art. 6(3)].
evidence: shall always be considered to be high-risk where the AI system performs profiling of natural persons
note: The profiling rule sits at the end of a long paragraph about the derogation.

label: AI Act Art. 99(3)
sentence: Using a prohibited AI practice can cost a company up to 7% of its worldwide annual turnover [AI Act Art. 99(3)].
evidence: up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover
note: The top tier of fines, for Article 5.

label: AI Act Annex III(4)(a)
sentence: A tool that screens CVs before a recruiter sees them is high-risk [AI Act Annex III(4)(a)].
evidence: to analyse and filter job applications
note: Paraphrase: 'screens CVs' for 'analyse and filter job applications'.

label: AI Act Art. 113
sentence: Most of the AI Act applies from 2 August 2026 [AI Act Art. 113].
note: The general application date, ahead of the article's exceptions.

label: GDPR Art. 33(1)
sentence: A personal data breach must normally be reported to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of it [GDPR Art. 33(1)].
evidence: not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it
note: The breach notification deadline.

label: GDPR Art. 35(1)
sentence: Before processing likely to result in a high risk to people's rights, the controller must assess its impact on data protection [GDPR Art. 35(1)].
evidence: shall, prior to the processing, carry out an assessment of the impact
note: When a DPIA is due.

label: GDPR Art. 22(1)
sentence: People have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing that significantly affects them [GDPR Art. 22(1)].
evidence: the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing
note: The automated-decision right.

label: GDPR Art. 3(2)
sentence: A company outside the EU that sells online to people in the EU is covered by the GDPR [GDPR Art. 3(2)].
evidence: by a controller or processor not established in the Union
note: The GDPR's extraterritorial rule, in plain words.

label: AI Act Art. 2(3)
sentence: The AI Act applies to providers outside the EU when the output of their AI system is used in the EU [AI Act Art. 2(3)].
note: From a live run: 2(3) is the national-security exclusion; the rule meant is 2(1)(c).

label: AI Act Art. 5(1)(f)
sentence: Using AI to read the emotions of shoppers in a store is prohibited [AI Act Art. 5(1)(f)].
note: The ban covers workplaces and education institutions, not shops.

label: AI Act Art. 50(1)
sentence: Deployers must disclose that a deep fake has been artificially generated [AI Act Art. 50(1)].
note: Same article, wrong paragraph: 50(1) is the chatbot duty of providers.

label: AI Act Art. 6(3)
sentence: An Annex III system that profiles people avoids being high-risk if it only performs a narrow procedural task [AI Act Art. 6(3)].
note: The provision says the opposite: profiling is always high-risk. The narrow-task condition is in it, which is the trap.

label: AI Act Art. 99(4)
sentence: Using a prohibited AI practice can cost up to 7% of worldwide annual turnover [AI Act Art. 99(4)].
note: 99(4) is the 3% tier, and excludes Article 5.

label: AI Act Art. 113
sentence: The obligations attached to Article 6(1) apply from 2 August 2026 [AI Act Art. 113].
note: Contradicted: point (c) of the same article says 2 August 2027.

label: AI Act Annex III(3)(a)
sentence: A tool that screens CVs before a recruiter sees them is high-risk [AI Act Annex III(3)(a)].
note: Point 3 is education; employment is point 4.

label: AI Act Art. 26(1)
sentence: Deployers of high-risk AI systems must carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment [AI Act Art. 26(1)].
note: 26(1) is using the system per its instructions; the assessment is 27(1), and only for some deployers.

label: GDPR Art. 34(1)
sentence: A data breach must be notified to the supervisory authority within 72 hours [GDPR Art. 34(1)].
note: 34(1) is telling the data subject, with no 72-hour limit.

label: GDPR Art. 15(1)
sentence: People can ask a company to delete their personal data [GDPR Art. 15(1)].
note: 15(1) is the right of access; erasure is 17(1).

label: GDPR Art. 6(1)(f)
sentence: Public authorities may rely on legitimate interests as the lawful basis for their tasks [GDPR Art. 6(1)(f)].
note: Point (f) says nothing about public authorities, and the article goes on to exclude them.

label: GDPR Art. 22(1)
sentence: All profiling requires the data subject's explicit consent [GDPR Art. 22(1)].
note: 22(1) restricts solely automated decisions with significant effects; it says nothing like this about profiling.
